name: Balangoda culture (Mesolithic Sri Lanka)
dateLabel: from before 34,000 BP to the Iron Age (c. 900 BCE); shown from 10,000 BCE
evidenceNote: No writing; known from cave deposits and skeletons dated by radiocarbon, and its end is poorly documented.
summary: The hunter-gatherers of Sri Lanka, named after Balangoda, where their remains were first found. They lived in caves such as Fa Hien and Batadomba lena and in open camps, made tiny geometric stone tools (microliths) far earlier than most of the world, hunted and gathered in the forests and may have kept dogs. Their way of life lasted until farming and iron reached the island in the early first millennium BCE.

name: Neolithic of Baluchistan (Mehrgarh)
dateLabel: c. 7000–4500 BCE (excavators); 2025 dates put the start near 5200 BCE
evidenceNote: The villages are excavated, but when farming began is debated: about 7000 BCE in the excavators' chronology, about 5200 BCE in new radiocarbon dates.
summary: The first farming villages of South Asia, on the Kachi plain and in the valleys of Baluchistan, Pakistan, best known from Mehrgarh. People grew wheat and barley, herded sheep, goats and zebu cattle, and built mudbrick houses and granaries; pottery came later. They traded shell and lapis lazuli over long distances. This way of life grew into the Chalcolithic cultures that led to the Indus civilisation.

sources.title: Mutin et al. 2025, Scientific Reports: new radiocarbon dates from Neolithic Mehrgarh (PMC)

name: Jeitun culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The earliest farmers of Central Asia, living in small villages of clay-block houses along the northern foothills of the Kopet Dag in Turkmenistan and the neighbouring Gorgan plain. They grew barley and wheat, kept sheep and goats and still hunted for part of their food. Their culture shows close links with early farming villages in Iran.

sources.title: Harris, Gosden & Charles 1996, Jeitun: recent excavations (Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society)

name: Kelteminar culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Neolithic hunters, gatherers and fishers of the Karakum and Kyzylkum deserts and the deltas of the Amu Darya and Zeravshan, in today's Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan. Whole communities of up to a hundred people could share one huge house, and over time they began to keep animals. The culture was first described in 1939 by the Soviet Khorezm expedition.

name: Early Harappan (Ravi, Kot Diji and Sothi-Siswal phases)
evidenceNote: No readable writing; known from excavated towns such as Kot Diji, Harappa and Kalibangan and from radiocarbon dates.
summary: The formative stage of the Indus civilisation, when regional farming cultures of the Indus plain, Baluchistan and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley grew into walled towns with shared pottery styles, early signs, standard bricks and long-distance trade. It is known by phases named after sites: Ravi and Hakra Ware, Kot Diji in Sindh and Punjab, and Sothi-Siswal on the Ghaggar. Around 2600 BCE these merged into the Mature Harappan civilisation. From about 3000 BCE the map shows the Indus civilisation as a state.

name: Southern Neolithic (Ashmound tradition)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The first farmers and herders of the Deccan, in today's Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, living near granite hills along the Tungabhadra, Krishna and Hagari rivers. They kept large herds of cattle, grew millets, and left great mounds of burnt cattle dung, the ashmounds, at sites such as Utnur, Kupgal and Budihal. Their culture gave way to the Iron Age megalith builders.

name: Ahar–Banas culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A Chalcolithic farming culture of south-eastern Rajasthan, along the Banas, Berach and Ahar rivers, contemporary with and next to the Indus civilisation. More than 90 sites are known, such as Ahar and Balathal. Its people mined the copper of the Aravalli hills for axes and tools, grew wheat and barley, and made distinctive black-and-red pottery painted in white.

name: Northern Neolithic (Kashmir)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The farming culture of the Kashmir Valley, known from Burzahom and Gufkral. Its people first lived in pits dug into the ground, later in houses at ground level, grew wheat, hunted deer and made polished stone axes and many bone tools. Stone harvesting knives and millet suggest contact with farmers of northern China across the mountains, while pottery and beads show links to the Indus world.

name: Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex (Oxus civilisation)
evidenceNote: No writing has been found; known from excavations of fortified towns and cemeteries and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Bronze Age civilisation of the oases of southern Central Asia, in the Murghab delta (Margiana) of Turkmenistan and along the upper Amu Darya (Bactria) in Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Tajikistan. Its people built fortified, square or round compounds of mudbrick such as Gonur Depe, irrigated their fields, and made fine metalwork and small stone figurines of seated women. They traded with Iran, Mesopotamia and the Indus. Its links to later Indo-Iranian speakers are debated.

name: Sintashta culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A Bronze Age culture of the steppe east of the southern Urals, in Russia and northern Kazakhstan. Its people lived in fortified settlements such as Sintashta and Arkaim, worked copper on a large scale, and buried their leaders with horses, weapons and the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots. Many scholars see it as the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages.

name: Andronovo culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A family of related Late Bronze Age cultures of herders and farmers across the Kazakh steppe, from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei and south to the edges of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. They kept cattle, horses, sheep, goats and camels, farmed where they could, and worked copper and bronze. Scholars widely link them with early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages.

name: Ochre Coloured Pottery culture (with the Copper Hoards)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A Bronze Age culture of the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab, eastern Punjab, Haryana and north-eastern Rajasthan, named after its orange-red pottery that rubs off on the fingers. It overlaps with the Late Harappans and is linked to hoards of copper weapons and tools. The cemetery of Sinauli, with its wheeled carts, belongs to it. It was followed by the Painted Grey Ware culture.

name: Late Harappan (Cemetery H, Jhukar and Rangpur phases)
evidenceNote: No readable writing; known from excavated villages and cemeteries and from radiocarbon dates.
summary: The phase after the great Indus cities declined, when settlement shifted east towards Haryana and the Ganga-Yamuna doab and south into Gujarat. Regional cultures replaced the shared urban style: Cemetery H in Punjab and Haryana, known for its painted burial jars, Jhukar in Sindh and Rangpur in Gujarat. Writing and seals faded, and people lived in smaller farming villages.

name: Malwa culture
dateLabel: c. 1600–1300 BCE (calibrated dates suggest a start as early as 2000–1750 BCE)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A Chalcolithic farming culture of the Malwa plateau in Madhya Pradesh and parts of northern Maharashtra, known from sites such as Navdatoli and Kayatha. Its people grew wheat, barley, pulses and later rice, kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, and painted their pottery in black on red. Most villages were unplanned clusters of houses, though the largest had walls.

name: Yaz culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The early Iron Age culture of Margiana, Bactria and Sogdia, which followed the BMAC. Its people lived in rural settlements around fortified mudbrick platforms and citadels, dug irrigation canals, and used hand-made and later wheel-made pottery with iron sickles and arrowheads. Burials almost disappear in this period, and many scholars link it to the early Iranian world of the Avesta.

name: Jorwe culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A Chalcolithic culture of the Deccan in Maharashtra, named after the village of Jorwe. Over 200 settlements are known, from farming villages to herders' camps; the largest, Daimabad, had a mud wall. Its people grew barley, wheat, millets and pulses, and made red pottery painted in black. Its villages suggest chiefdoms rather than states.

name: Gandhara grave culture (Swat protohistoric graves)
dateLabel: c. 1400–800 BCE in Swat (Italian mission); some scholars extend it to the historic period
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavated sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A protohistoric culture of north-western Pakistan known mainly from large cemeteries in the middle Swat valley, spreading to Dir, Chitral and Peshawar. The dead were mostly buried, sometimes cremated, in stone-lined graves with pottery and ornaments. Ancient DNA from these graves shows people of Indus-related and steppe-related ancestry mixing in the second millennium BCE.

name: Painted Grey Ware culture
evidenceNote: No writing; known from about 1,500 excavated or surveyed sites and radiocarbon dates; links to the Vedic texts are proposed, not proven.
summary: An Iron Age culture of the western Ganga plain and the Ghaggar-Hakra valley, named after its fine grey pottery painted with black geometric designs. Its people lived in villages and small towns, kept horses, worked ivory and iron, and grew rice, wheat and barley. Many scholars connect it with the later Vedic period and the Kuru and Panchala lands; it gave way to the cities of the Mahajanapadas.

name: Iron Age megalithic cultures of South India
dateLabel: c. 1200 BCE–200 CE; shown until c. 300 BCE, when the Sangam kingdoms appear on the map
evidenceNote: Mostly known from thousands of excavated tombs dated by radiocarbon; Tamil-Brahmi writing appears only near the end.
summary: Iron Age peoples of peninsular India who buried their dead, or their bones, in stone-built tombs: dolmens, stone circles, cists and large pottery urns, as at Hire Benakal and Adichanallur. Graves hold iron weapons and tools, black-and-red pottery and beads. These communities of farmers, herders and craftsmen form the background to the early Tamil kingdoms of the Sangam age.
